bib.title: Introduction to Information Retrieval, Chapter 20: Web crawling and indexes
bib.venue: Cambridge University Press (online edition, draft April 1, 2009)

question: How is a web crawler built (robust, polite, distributed, fresh), and how are indexes and the link graph distributed and stored across machines?
contributions: Mercator-style crawler architecture, DNS resolution and URL frontier (20.2)
Term vs document partitioning of indexes (20.3)
Connectivity servers with compressed web graph (20.4)

results.claim: Fetching a billion pages in a month-long crawl needs several hundred fetches per second.
results.setup: Reference point for crawler design, 2008-2009 web size; no derivation shown (1e9/30 days is about 386/s)
results.quote: fetching a billion pages (a small fraction of the static Web at present) in a month-long crawl requires fetching several hundred pages each second

results.claim: Mercator recommends roughly three times as many back queues as crawler threads in the URL frontier.
results.setup: Politeness/priority URL frontier with F front queues and B back queues
results.quote: The designers of Mercator recommend a rough rule of three times as many back queues as crawler threads.

results.claim: Politeness heuristic: gap between successive fetches to a host should be an order of magnitude larger than the last fetch time; example next-allowed time is now plus ten times the last fetch time.
results.quote: A common heuristic is to insert a gap between successive fetch requests to a host that is an order of magnitude larger than the time taken for the most recent fetch from that host.
results.note: Separately says a wait of 'a few seconds' between requests to a host (p.445, p.451); the two rules differ and the chapter does not reconcile them. Exercise 20.3 asks how the 10x and 3x constants relate.

results.claim: Mercator DNS resolver retries about five times with an exponentially growing wait, from one second to roughly 90 seconds.
results.setup: Custom asynchronous DNS resolver, because library lookups are synchronous and block threads; some host names take tens of seconds to resolve
results.quote: the designers of Mercator recommend of the order of ﬁve attempts
results.note: Start and end waits are in the text: 'Mercator started with one second and ended with roughly 90 seconds'.

results.claim: Naive web graph storage for four billion pages with ten links each needs 3.2 x 10^11 bytes.
results.setup: 4 billion pages, 10 out-links each, 32-bit (4-byte) integer per link end
results.note: Printed with lost superscripts (109, 1011) in the extracted text.

results.claim: An adjacency-table representation halves the naive link storage.
results.setup: Row per page with sorted list of linked page integers vs two 32-bit endpoints per link
results.quote: This table representation cuts the space taken by the naive representation

results.claim: With prototype-row, locality and gap encoding, the connectivity server uses as few as 3 bits per link versus 64 naive.
results.setup: Rows encoded against one of seven preceding rows (3-bit offset), gap encoded; experiments cited in 20.5 (Boldi and Vigna 2004a;b); naive is 64 bits
results.quote: appears to use as few as 3 bits per link, on average
results.note: Text also says 'well under 10%' of the naive memory; 3/64 is about 4.7%.

results.claim: Expressing each row against one of seven preceding rows lets the offset fit in 3 bits.
results.setup: Row-prototype encoding of the link table
results.quote: the offset can be expressed with only 3 bits; this choice is optimized empirically
results.note: Seventh not eighth because one code is needed for 'no prototype' (Exercise 20.4).

results.claim: Document partitioning of a distributed index is generally found better than term partitioning when term distribution is skewed, but at least one line of work found the opposite.
results.setup: Comparisons by Tomasic and Garcia-Molina 1993, Jeong and Omiecinski 1995, MacFarlane et al. 2000; counter: Ribeiro-Neto and Barbosa 1998, Badue et al. 2001
results.quote: Document partitioning is found to be superior, at least when the distribution of terms is skewed, as it typically is in practice.

limits: Dated: 2008 web (a billion pages 'a small fraction of the static Web'); four-billion-page example; IPv4 only, IPv6 mentioned as future.
Static HTML crawling; no JavaScript rendering, dynamic or deep-web pages, sitemaps or crawl-delay directives; robots.txt example only Disallow.
No measured experiments in the chapter; numbers are design rules or worked arithmetic, and 3 bits/link is quoted from other work.
Freshness is stated as a goal (crawl at the page change rate) with only a priority-by-change-rate heuristic; no refresh-policy analysis.
Says it does not describe a full-scale commercial crawler.
Document-vs-term partitioning outcome 'depends on the details of the distributed system'.
practices: Open only one connection per host at a time and wait a few seconds between requests to a host (p.445).
Obey robots.txt, and filter against it immediately before fetching, not at enqueue time, because a URL can wait days or weeks in the frontier (p.447).
Cache robots.txt per host; locality in dequeued URLs still gives high hit rates (p.447).
Detect duplicate content with checksum fingerprints or shingles; store the fingerprint in the frontier so it can be deleted on re-crawl (p.446, 449).
Partition crawl by host, not URL, using a host splitter before the duplicate URL eliminator (p.448; Exercises 20.1-20.2).
Use own asynchronous DNS resolver with a cache, retries about five times and exponential timeouts (p.450).
Prioritise by both change rate and quality since spam pages change on every fetch (p.451).
Use front queues for priority and back queues (one host each) with a heap of earliest-contact times for politeness (p.451-453).
Keep most of a large frontier on disk with a portion of each queue in memory (p.453).
Checkpoint crawler state every few hours (p.448).
Partition a serving index by documents, hash URLs to nodes for even load, query all nodes and merge top k; refresh global idf by background processes (p.454-455).
Split documents into high-scoring and low-scoring indexes and search the latter only when matches are too few (p.455).
